Finally, the parties to such an agreement would remain subject only to the laws of nature in relation to one another, with no guarantee that either would honour the promises made. That is entirely at odds with civil society. Only the stronger party could force the other to fulfil the agreement. We might as well call it a contract if someone said to another, “I give you all my property on the condition that you return as much of it as you choose.”
A state has only one compact: the act of association, which excludes all others. We cannot imagine any later public contract that would not violate the original one from the beginning.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. XVII. Of the institution of government.
paragraphs: What, then, should we understand by the act that establishes government? I will begin by pointing out that it has two parts: setting down the law and carrying it out in the political order.
In the first, the sovereign enacts that government should be established in a particular form. Since this is a general act, it is plainly a law.

In the second, the people choose the leaders who will administer the government just established. This choice concerns particular persons, so it is not another law but a consequence of the first one: in fact, an act of government.

The difficulty is understanding how an act of government can occur before government exists, and how people, who must always be either sovereign or subjects, can in certain circumstances become prince or magistrate.

Here we discover one of the political body’s astonishing abilities: it can reconcile actions that seem to contradict one another. It does this by suddenly changing sovereign authority into a democracy. Without any noticeable change, only through a new relation of everyone to everyone else, citizens become magistrates and move from general acts to particular ones, from making laws to carrying them out.

This change in relations is not merely a theoretical idea with no real example. It happens often in the British Parliament: on certain questions the whole House of Commons becomes a committee, allowing members to examine and debate the matter more effectively. They then act only as commissioners of the sovereign court they had formed a moment before. When the inquiry is over, they report to themselves, now as the House of Commons, on what they decided as a committee, and begin deliberating again under the former name about matters already settled under the latter.

This is the particular advantage of a democratic government: in practice, the simple act of the general will establishes it. The provisional government then continues if that is the intended form; otherwise it establishes, in the sovereign’s name, the form of government adopted by law. Everything then proceeds in order. There is no other lawful way to establish a government without abandoning the principles set out earlier.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. XVIII. Of the means of preventing the usurpations of government.
paragraphs: The points just explained confirm what I argued in Chapter XVI: the act establishing government is a law, not a contract. Those entrusted with executive power are the people’s servants, not their masters. The people may appoint or remove them whenever they wish. These officials cannot claim any contract with the people; they must obey them. By accepting the offices the state gives them, they merely fulfil their duty as citizens and have no right to dispute the terms.

If the people set up hereditary government—either a monarchy limited to one family or an aristocracy held by a particular order of citizens—they make no formal contract. They merely give the administration a temporary form, which remains lawful until they choose to change it.

Such changes are certainly dangerous, and an established government should not be disturbed unless it proves harmful to the public good. But this caution is a rule of policy, not a question of right. The state is no more bound to hand civil authority to its magistrates or leaders than it is to entrust military authority to its generals.

Great care must also be taken to observe every formality needed to distinguish a proper, lawful act from a seditious disturbance, and the whole people’s general will from a faction’s shouting. In the latter case, the people should give even the best-supported protests no more attention than strict justice requires. But a prince can exploit this duty to preserve his power against the people without appearing to usurp it. By seeming only to exercise his legitimate powers, he can extend them and, in the name of preserving public order, stop the meetings that might restore proper government. He can benefit from keeping the silence unbroken and from irregularities he has caused himself, claiming that those who remain silent approve while punishing anyone bold enough to speak. This is how the decemvirs, first elected for a single year and then kept for another, tried to make their power permanent: they prevented the comitia from meeting as usual. In these simple ways, every government, once it holds power, eventually usurps sovereign authority This is why public oversight must remain active even between assemblies, and why legal procedure matters most when political tempers are high.

The regular assemblies I mentioned earlier are well suited to prevent or delay this disaster, especially when they need no special summons. The prince cannot stop them without openly declaring himself a lawbreaker and enemy of the state.
The opening of these assemblies, whose sole purpose is to preserve the social compact, should always include two proposals. Neither can be omitted, and they must be voted on separately.
First: Is it the sovereign’s decision to keep the present form of government?
Second: Does the people wish to leave the administration in the hands of those now responsible for it in the state.

I assume here, as I believe I have already proved, that no fundamental law in any state is beyond repeal, not even the social compact itself. If all the citizens assembled together and agreed to end that compact, it would certainly be dissolved by lawful means. Grotius even believes that a person may leave the state to which he belongs, recover his natural independence and property, and return to them. It would be absurd to think that all citizens acting together could not do what any one of them may do alone.

There is one exception: a person must not flee merely to escape his duty or avoid serving his country in an emergency when his help is needed. In that case, flight would be criminal and deserve severe punishment. It would be desertion, not withdrawal.

chapters.title: Book IV. CHAP. I. That the general will cannot be annihilated.
paragraphs: As long as people remain closely united and regard themselves as one body, they can have only one will, directed towards their shared preservation and welfare. The state’s resources are then simple and strong, and its political principles clear and obvious. No tangled or opposing interests compete; the public good is plain to everyone and requires only ordinary good sense to recognize. Peace, agreement, and equality leave no room for political tricks. When people are honest and straightforward, their simplicity protects them from deception. They are too direct to be fooled by false arguments. If the happiest people in the world can have their farmers gather under an oak tree and manage public affairs with the greatest care, how can we avoid looking down on nations that use so much artifice and secrecy only to make themselves magnificently unhappy?

A state governed so simply needs only a few laws. Whenever a new one is needed, that need is clear to everyone. The first person to propose it merely puts into words what all have already thought. No eloquence or scheming is needed to pass a law everyone had already decided to support once they knew others would do the same.

What misleads those who reason about this subject is that they have seen only states that were badly designed from the beginning. They are struck by how impossible it would be to keep public affairs simple in such places. They laugh at the thought of a scheming rascal or persuasive speaker leading the people of Paris or London into absurdity. They do not realize that at Berne or Geneva, Cromwell or Beaufort would have been treated as troublemakers and punished as they deserved.

But when social bonds begin to loosen and the state grows weak, private interests appear and factions begin to influence it. The public good meets resistance. Agreement no longer rules the people’s assemblies; the general will no longer coincides with everyone’s will. Contradictions and arguments arise, and even the best advice meets opposition Their disagreement grows harder to settle as interests diverge.

When the state is near collapse and survives only in name, when social ties no longer connect people’s hearts, and the basest self-interest shamelessly takes the sacred name of public good, the general will falls silent. Individuals act for private ends, with no more feeling as citizens than if the state had never existed. A sham legislature then passes unjust decrees as laws, serving nothing but private interest.

Does this mean that the general will has disappeared or become corrupt? No. It remains constant, unchanging, and pure, though the will of a faction overrules it. There is nobody who, when separating his own interest from the public’s, does not see that he cannot separate himself completely. But his share of the common harm seems small compared with the benefit he hopes to secure for himself alone. Apart from this motive, he is as ready as anyone to support measures for the public good, even for his own sake. Even when he sells his vote, he does not lose all awareness of the general will; he merely evades it. His fault is to change the question and answer something nobody asked. Instead of voting on whether a measure serves the state’s interest, he votes on whether a particular person’s or faction’s interest is served by passing a law. Public assemblies should therefore be organized not only to protect the general will from violation, but to ensure that it is always asked for and always gives an answer.

I could say more about the basic right to vote on every act of sovereignty, a right no citizen can be denied; and about the rights to think, propose, and debate public matters, which government is always eager to reserve to its own members. But this subject is important enough to deserve a treatise of its own, and I cannot cover everything here.

chapters.title: Book IV. CHAP. II. On Votes.
paragraphs: As the previous chapter showed, the way public business is handled gives a reliable sign of a people’s customs and the political body’s health. The more agreement there is in public meetings—that is, the closer members come to unanimous votes—the more strongly the general will prevails. Long debates, divisions, and disturbances show that private interests are taking control and the state is weakening across public decisions in public decisions.

This may seem less clear when a constitution has two or more orders of people, as at Rome, where conflicts between patricians and plebeians often disturbed the comitia even when the republic was flourishing. But this is more an apparent than a real exception. A defect in the political body has produced two states within one, and what is not true of both together can still be true of each separately. In fact, even in the republic’s most turbulent times, plebeian decisions passed peacefully by majority vote when the Senate did not interfere. Since citizens shared one interest, the people could have only one will.

Unanimity appears again at the opposite end of the cycle, when citizens have been reduced to slavery and no longer possess liberty or will. Fear and flattery turn their votes into cheers. They no longer deliberate with one another; they either praise or curse their tyrants. Such were the degraded rules of the Senate under Rome’s emperors. Even the public’s feelings were often expressed with absurd caution. Tacitus says that under Otho, while the senators cursed Vitellius, they deliberately made a confused uproar so he could not learn who had said what if he became their master.

From these points we can draw principles for counting votes and comparing them, according to how easily the general will can be found and how far the state has declined. Only one kind of law requires unanimous consent by its nature: the social compact. Civil association is the most voluntary act in the world. Everyone is born free and master of himself, so nobody may be restrained on any grounds without his own consent. To say that the child of a slave is born a slave is to say that he is not born a human being.

If some people oppose the compact itself, their opposition does not cancel it; it only prevents them from being included in it. They remain foreigners among citizens. When a state is founded, someone’s consent to it is inferred from his residence: choosing to live in a country means accepting its sovereignty.

This applies only to a free state, where people may leave whenever they want and take their property with them. Elsewhere, family ties, property, having nowhere else to go, necessity, or force may keep someone in a country against his will. In that case mere residence does not imply consent to the compact or a breach of it.

Except for this original agreement, a majority decision always binds the rest; that follows necessarily from the compact itself. But how can a person be free and still have to follow other people’s will? How can members of an opposition be called free when they are forced to obey laws they did not support? I answer that the question is wrongly framed. A citizen consents to every law adopted by a majority, even if a particular law passed against his wishes—and even if the law punishes him for breaking one. The lasting will shared by all members of the state is the general will, and only that will makes them citizens and free people. When a law is proposed in the assembly, citizens are not exactly asked whether each personally likes it. They are asked whether it agrees with the general will, which is theirs as a collective body. Each vote states a judgment on that question, and the majority reveals what the general will is. If the law passes against my opinion, that proves only that I was mistaken about the general will. Had my personal advice been followed, it would have gone against my will as a citizen, which is the same as the general will; in that case I would not have been free.

In Genoa the word *Libertas* is written on the chains of galley slaves and on prison doors. The emblem is apt and just: in every state it is criminals who violate citizens’ liberty. A country where all wrongdoers were actually chained to the oar would be a country of perfect freedom at any time.
This argument assumes that a majority vote always contains every defining feature of the general will. When that stops being true, liberty ends, whatever one may do within the state.

By explaining how the wills of individuals and factions replace the general will in public deliberation, I have already pointed out practical ways to prevent this abuse; I will say more later. I have also set out the principles for deciding what number of votes reflects the general will. A difference of one vote is enough to end unanimity, but there are many possible ratios between unanimity and an exact tie. The political body’s circumstances determine which proportion is suitable in public meetings.

Two broad principles can guide these proportions. The more serious and important the decision, the closer the required vote should be to unanimity. The more urgently a matter must be decided, the less we should demand unanimity. When a decision cannot wait, a majority of one vote should suffice. The first principle seems to fit lasting laws best, the second ordinary business. In any event, the right balance of these principles determines what majority should count as the general will for the political community and every voter in practice.

chapters.title: Book IV. CHAP. III. Of Elections.
paragraphs: Choosing a prince or magistrate, as I observed earlier, is a complex act. There are two ways to do it: by selection or by lot. Different republics have used both, and in our own time Venice uses a complicated combination of the two to choose its doge in public affairs.

Montesquieu says selection by lot is democratic. I agree, though not for the reason he gives. He says a lottery offends nobody because every citizen can reasonably hope to be chosen for service to his country in their service.

That is not the true explanation. If we remember that choosing leaders is a governmental function, not an act of sovereignty, we can see why sortition suits democracy: the fewer administrative decisions it requires, the better its government works as government.

In a genuine democracy, being a magistrate is not a privilege but a difficult, costly duty. It would be unjust to impose that burden on one person instead of another. The law therefore assigns it to the person whose name is drawn. Since everyone has an equal chance, the choice does not depend on someone’s personal will, and no private appeal can alter the law’s universal rule.

In an aristocracy, the prince chooses its leaders, since the government provides for itself; this is where voting is properly used. The doge’s election in Venice may seem an exception, but it confirms the distinction: the Venetians’ mixed procedure suits their mixed government. Venice is not a true aristocracy. Although the lower ranks do not govern, the nobility takes their place and becomes the people in relation to administration. Many of the lesser nobles have no chance of entering government; their rank gives them little beyond the empty title of “Excellency” and a seat in the Great Council. That council is about as large as Geneva’s general council, so its illustrious members have no greater rights than Geneva’s ordinary citizens. Apart from the great difference in size between the republics, Geneva’s burghers correspond exactly to Venice’s patricians; our native residents and temporary residents correspond to their citizens and people; our peasants correspond to those living in Venice’s mainland territories. However we view Venice, once we set aside its grandeur, its government is no more aristocratic than Geneva’s. The only difference is that Geneva does not need this kind of election.

Sortition causes little trouble in a true democracy, where people are nearly equal in customs, ability, judgment, and wealth, and it makes little difference who is chosen. But, as I have already said, a true democracy is only an ideal.

When an election combines voting and lot, votes should choose officials who need special abilities, as in military affairs. Lot is better for offices requiring only common sense, honesty, and integrity, such as judicial positions, since in a well-formed state all citizens share those qualities in public service to service.

Neither voting nor sortition is used under monarchy. The monarch alone is the lawful prince and magistrate, so only he may choose a substitute. When the Abbé de Saint-Pierre proposed expanding the French king’s councils and electing their members by ballot, he did not realize that this would change the form of the French government in the state.

I still need to discuss how votes are cast and counted in popular assemblies. But a historical account of Roman practice may explain it better than any principles I could offer. A thoughtful reader should take the time to see how they handled both general and particular matters in an assembly of two hundred thousand people of the assembly.

chapters.title: Book IV. CHAP. IV. Of the Roman Comitia.
paragraphs: We have no reliable records from Rome’s earliest years, and there is strong reason to think most of the stories told about them are inventions. The most interesting and instructive part of any nation’s history—its beginnings—is usually the least complete. We see each day what causes kingdoms and empires to change, but because we have no examples of states being founded before our eyes, we can only make guesses about their origins.

Rome’s name is said to come from Romulus, but it is Greek for “strength”; Numa’s name is Greek too, meaning “law.” How likely is it that the first two kings of the city happened to bear names that so precisely anticipated what they would do?

The customs that were actually established are enough to show that they must have begun somehow. Of the traditions about their origins, those that seem most reasonable and best supported should be taken as the most reliable. These are the principles I have followed in tracing how the most powerful and free people in the world exercised sovereignty.

After Rome was founded, the young republic—that is, the founder’s army of Albans, Sabines, and foreigners—was divided into three groups called tribes. Each tribe was then split into ten curiae, and each curia into decuries, each headed by a leader called a curio or decurio Each subdivision had a named leader.

Each tribe also supplied a hundred cavalrymen, or knights, known as centurions. Since these divisions were not necessary to organize a city’s ordinary life, they must at first have been purely military. Yet perhaps the small town of Rome already anticipated its future greatness and adopted an administrative system fit for the capital of the world.

This original division soon caused a problem. The Alban and Sabine tribes stayed the same size, while the foreign tribe kept growing as newcomers arrived and soon outnumbered the other two. Servius dealt with the dangerous imbalance by changing the system. He abolished distinctions of ancestry and divided people according to the part of the city where each tribe lived. In place of three tribes he created four, each settled on one of Rome’s hills and named after it. By removing the inequality at the time, he prevented it from arising again. To make the division geographic as well as personal, he barred people from moving from one quarter to another and thus kept families from mixing while the foreign population continued to grow.

He also doubled the original three cavalry centuries and added twelve more, keeping the old name. This simple, sensible choice distinguished the knights from the people without provoking complaints from the latter without changing the name attached to the corps.

Servius then added fifteen more tribes to the four city tribes. These were called rural tribes, since they were made up of people from the countryside, divided into the same number of districts. In time, an equal number of new divisions was added, and the Roman people came to be divided into thirty-five tribes. This number remained fixed until the republic finally fell.

The distinction between city and rural tribes had an important effect: we have no other example like it, and Rome owed to it both the preservation of its customs and the growth of its empire. We might expect city tribes to seize power and honours for themselves and scorn the rural people. The opposite happened. Everyone knows the ancient Romans’ fondness for country life. They learned it from the wise founder who linked liberty with the work of farmer and soldier, while leaving the city, so to speak, to the arts, trade, scheming, wealth, and slavery.

The most prominent Romans lived in the country and worked at farming, and the Romans looked to these people alone to defend the republic. Everyone respected this status, held by the most worthy patricians. The plain, hard-working life of the farmer was valued above the mean, idle life of a city dweller. Even someone who had farmed in the country and later became a respectable householder in the city was still looked down on. Varro rightly says that our great-hearted ancestors established in the countryside a nursery for the strong, brave men who defended them in war and cared for them in peace. Pliny explicitly says rural tribes were honoured because of the people who belonged to them, while anyone who deserved disgrace was moved into a city tribe. When Appius Claudius the Sabine settled in Rome, he was showered with honours and enrolled in a rural tribe, which later took his family’s name. Finally, freed people were always registered in city tribes, never rural ones. During the republic’s entire existence, not one of them was ever chosen for magistracy, even after becoming a citizen.
This was an excellent principle, though taken so far that it changed the state’s administration and certainly became an abuse.

At first, censors claimed the right to move citizens from one tribe to another as they pleased. Later they allowed most people to register in any tribe they chose. This could serve no good purpose and deprived the censors of one of their strongest tools of discipline. The wealthy then put themselves in rural tribes, while freed people and the common population filled the city tribes. The tribes no longer represented particular places; they became so mixed that only the registers could show who belonged where. The meaning of “tribe” therefore shifted from a place to a group of people—or became entirely imaginary.
The city tribes, being nearer, generally held the most influence in the comitia and treated the state as their property, selling votes to anyone base enough to buy them among the people taking part.

Each tribe had ten curiae, making thirty in all among the Roman people inside the walls. Every curia had its own temples, gods, officers, and festivals called Compitalia, similar to the Paganalia later established for the rural tribes.

When Servius created his four tribes, thirty could not be divided evenly among them, so he left the curiae unchanged. They became a separate division of the people, independent of the tribes. There were no curiae among the rural tribes or the people who made them up. Once the tribes became a civic institution and troops were raised by another method, Romulus’s military divisions were unnecessary. Thus every citizen was recorded in a tribe, but many belonged to no curia. Servius made a third division unrelated to the first two, and it became the most important. He divided the Roman people into six classes based on property, not ancestry or residence. The wealthy filled the higher classes, the poor the lowest, and people of moderate means the middle ones. The classes were split into 193 smaller groups called centuries. These were arranged so that the first class alone held more than half the centuries, while the sixth and lowest had just one. The smallest class by population therefore had the most centuries; the last class was numerically only a subdivision even though it included more than half of Rome’s people.

Servius tried to make this last arrangement look military so the people would not notice its purpose. He placed two centuries of armourers in the second class and assigned two military instruments to the fourth. In every class except the last, he also separated the young from the old: those required to bear arms from those excused because of age. This meant the census had to be repeated more often than changes in property alone would require. Finally, he ordered the assembly to meet on the Field of Mars, where all those old enough for military service had to appear armed They were called to appear with their arms.

He made no age distinction within the last class because the common people in it were not allowed the honour of bearing arms for their country. A man had to own a house before he could earn the right to defend himself. Among the vast armies that make modern princes look so splendid, there may not be one ordinary soldier who, for lack of property, would not have been contemptuously rejected from a Roman cohort, where soldiers defended liberty.

The last class still distinguished between people called proletarians and those counted only by their heads. The former had not fallen to absolute poverty and could at least give the state citizens, sometimes soldiers in an emergency. Those with no property at all could be counted only by number and were disregarded; Marius was the first to enlist them.

I will not decide here whether this third kind of division was good or bad in itself. I can safely say, however, that only the simple customs of the ancient Romans—their public spirit, love of farming, and disdain for trade and profit—could have made it workable. What modern nation, with its ravenous greed, restless temper, trickery, and constant shifts in property, could keep such a system for twenty years without overthrowing the state? It should also be clear that Rome’s pure customs and a system of discipline more powerful than the institution itself corrected its flaws. A rich man could be removed from his own class and placed among the poor for making an improper show of his wealth.

This explains why people rarely speak of more than five classes, though there were actually six. The sixth supplied no soldiers to the army and no voters to the Field of Mars, and was so little use to the republic that it was scarcely counted.

I mention the Field of Mars because the comitia assembled by centuries there. In the other two kinds of assembly, they met in the forum and elsewhere, where those counted only by their heads had as much influence as the leading citizens.

These were the Roman people’s different divisions. We can now examine the shortcomings of their assemblies. When lawfully convened, they were called comitia and met on the Field of Mars or elsewhere in Rome. There were three forms—curiate, centuriate, and tribal—corresponding to the divisions into curiae, centuries, and tribes. Romulus established the curiate comitia, Servius the centuriate, and the people’s tribunes the tribal. No law could pass and no magistrate could be chosen outside the comitia. Since every citizen was registered in a curia, century, or tribe, nobody was excluded from voting. In law and in practice, the Roman people were therefore truly sovereign in the republic.

Three conditions were needed for a comitia to be lawfully assembled and its decisions to carry the force of law. First, the magistrate or body calling it had to possess the authority to do so. Second, it had to be held on a day permitted by law. Third, the omens had to favour its meeting.

The first requirement needs no explanation. The second was a matter of public administration: comitia could not meet on market days, when country people came to Rome on business and would otherwise be prevented from conducting it. The third requirement allowed the Senate to restrain a fierce, unruly crowd and properly curb the zeal of seditious tribunes. The tribunes nevertheless found several ways around this device.

The comitia decided more than laws and the choice of leaders. The Roman people had taken over the most important duties of government, so the fate of Europe could be said to depend on their assemblies. Since the matters brought before them varied, the form of each assembly was changed to suit its purpose.

We can understand the differences by comparing the systems. Romulus created the curiae to restrain the Senate through the people, the people through the Senate, and to keep equal influence over both for himself. This arrangement gave the people the advantage of numbers to balance the patricians’ power and wealth. Yet in keeping with monarchy, he gave patricians an advantage by letting their clients help them secure a majority of votes. This remarkable institution of patrons and clients combined political skill with humanity. Without it, the patrician order, so contrary to the spirit of the republic, could not have survived. Rome alone deserves credit for this fine example, which is not known to have been abused and was never adopted elsewhere as one institutional design.

The curiate division survived under the kings until Servius. Because the last Tarquin’s reign was considered unlawful, the royal laws came to be known generally as *leges curiatae* in the public order.

Under the republic, the curiae remained limited to the four city tribes and contained only Rome’s common people. They could not gain a seat in the Senate, led by the patricians, or become tribunes, who, though plebeians, represented citizens of means. The curiae therefore fell into contempt and were reduced to such insignificance that their thirty lictors did all the work of the curiate comitia itself.

The century system so strongly favoured aristocracy that it is at first hard to understand why the Senate did not always win in the centuriate comitia, where consuls, censors, and praetors were chosen. Of the 193 centuries across all six classes, the first class had 98. Since votes were counted by centuries, this one class had more votes than all the rest combined. When its centuries agreed, counting stopped; whatever the minority decided was treated as the mob’s opinion. It is fair to say that the centuriate comitia were governed more by wealth than by the number of votes Its upper class could settle the result through its own agreement before the other classes were counted.

Two things limited this overwhelming power. First, the tribunes and a significant number of wealthy citizens belonged to this rich class, balancing the patricians’ influence there. Second, the centuries did not vote in order of rank. Lots were drawn to choose which century would vote first. The selected century voted alone, while the others were summoned on another day to vote in order, usually confirming its choice. This practice set rank aside and gave preference to chance, in keeping with democratic principles The order of voting therefore depended on chance rather than status, giving each group an opportunity to speak first while preserving a later, broader confirmation among the votes.
The century chosen by lot was called *praerogativa*, because it was asked for its vote first. This is where the word “prerogative” comes from.

The practice had another benefit: country citizens had time between the two elections to learn about the candidates provisionally chosen and make a more informed decision. In time the practice was abolished under the excuse of speeding up business, and both elections were held on the same day before the final decision.

The tribal comitia were, properly speaking, the Roman people’s great council. Only tribunes called them; they also elected tribunes and passed plebiscites, or laws made by the people. Senators had no rank in these assemblies and could not even attend. They had to obey laws they had no part in making, leaving them less free in this respect than the lowest citizen. This injustice was poorly understood, but by itself was enough to invalidate decisions made by an assembly that excluded some of its members. If all patricians had attended as citizens, they could have exerted no improper influence, since every vote—from the poorest person to the greatest state official—would have counted equally This exclusion made the process unequal in law.

It is clear, then, that beyond the orderly way these divisions helped collect votes from a huge population, each system had its own effects. Their forms were not interchangeable; each suited particular aims better than the others Each division answered a different political purpose.

Without going into every detail, we can see that the tribal comitia best supported popular government, while the centuriate comitia favoured aristocracy. The curiate comitia, whose majority was made up of common people, served no useful purpose except to support tyrannical plans. They remained in the contemptible condition into which they had fallen; even plotters avoided using them because doing so would expose their designs too openly. The Roman people displayed their full majesty only in the complete centuriate comitia. The curiate lacked the rural tribes, while the tribal comitia excluded the Senate and patricians in practice.

Voting among the early Romans was as straightforward as their customs, though still less simple than in Sparta. Each person stated his vote aloud and the clerk recorded it. A majority in each tribe decided that tribe’s vote; the majority among the tribes decided the people’s vote. The same process applied to curiae and centuries. This worked well while citizens were honest and felt ashamed to publicly support an unworthy person or cause. But when people became corrupt and sold their votes, they had to vote in private instead, making it harder for buyers to trust that their orders would be followed and giving dishonest voters a way not to betray their own side.

I know Cicero condemns this change and blames it largely for the republic’s ruin. Despite the weight of his authority, I disagree. I think the state would have fallen more quickly if the Romans had not changed the voting system. A healthy person’s diet is not suitable for someone sick; it is just as foolish to govern a corrupt people under the same laws that suited them before their corruption. The long life of the Venetian republic proves this principle: its shadow survives only because its laws were designed for bad people Laws must fit the actual condition of a people.

When the voting method changed, citizens received tablets to cast their votes anonymously. Other methods were then needed to count and compare them: officials tallied the voices and checked the totals against the tablets. These methods did not prevent frequent suspicions that election officers were biased. The many laws later passed against election bribery show that they never solved the problem But no procedure entirely removed suspicion or the chance of error, and disputes continued through later elections.
The officials were called *custodes, diribitores, rogatores,* and *suffragiorum* collectors.

Toward the republic’s decline, extraordinary devices were tried because the laws were no longer sufficient. Officials sometimes staged omens successfully; this trick fooled the crowd but not those who guided it. At other times they called meetings at the last moment so candidates had no time to build unfair support. Sometimes they spent an entire session making speeches when they saw the people leaning towards the wrong side. In the end ambition escaped every safeguard. Yet, almost incredibly, amid all these abuses, this immense people continued under its ancient laws to elect magistrates, pass laws, judge cases, and conduct public and private business as easily as the Senate itself despite the state’s growing corruption in the assemblies.

chapters.title: Book IV. CHAP. V. On a Tribunate.
paragraphs: When it is impossible to set an exact balance among a state’s parts, or unavoidable causes keep changing their relations, a special office is created. It does not merge with the other parts but restores each to its proper relation. It acts as a middle force between prince and people, between prince and sovereign, or, when needed, between both at once.

I will call this body a tribunate. It safeguards the laws and legislative authority. At times it protects the sovereign from government, as Rome’s tribunes of the people did; at other times it protects government from the people, as Venice’s Council of Ten does now; or it can balance both sides, as Sparta’s ephors did in the constitutional balance overall.

The tribunate is not a constitutional part of the city and should therefore take no part in either legislative or executive power. Yet its own power is considerable: though it can do nothing itself, it can prevent others from acting. As defender of the laws it is more sacred and respected than the prince who enforces them or the sovereign who makes them. This was clear at Rome, where arrogant patricians, who always looked down on the people as a body, still had to yield to the people’s officers, though those officers had neither command nor jurisdiction.

When carefully kept in balance, the tribunate is the strongest support for a good constitution. But if it gains even a little too much power, it overturns everything. Its weakness is not a danger, since as long as it exists at all, it cannot have too little power.

The tribunate becomes tyrannical when it takes over the executive authority it should only regulate, or interprets laws it should only protect. The ephors’ immense power caused no harm while Sparta’s customs remained sound; once they began to decay, it only increased the corruption. Those tyrants killed Agis, and his successor took revenge for the murder. The ephors’ crime and punishment both hastened the republic’s fall: after Cleomenes, Sparta was nothing. Rome’s republic was destroyed in the same way. The tribunes gradually seized excessive power and eventually used laws passed in liberty’s defence to help secure the emperors who destroyed it. Venice’s Council of Ten is a bloodthirsty tribunal, hated equally by patricians and people. Far from openly protecting the laws, it now works in secret to break them It restrains power without creating a separate ruling authority.

Increasing the number of its members weakens the tribunate just as it weakens government. When Rome’s tribunes, first two and later five, wanted to double their number, the Senate did not object. It was confident it could make the tribunes restrain one another, and that is what happened.

The best way to prevent such a formidable body from usurping power—a method no government has yet used—would be to make it temporary and set periods when it must dissolve. These intervals should not be long enough for abuses to become established habits, and the law should allow them to be shortened by an extraordinary order when necessary lawfully when needed.

I can see no harm in this method. As I have said, the tribunate is not an essential part of the constitution and can be suspended without injury. The method should work as well, because a magistrate restored to office does not inherit the power of his predecessor but only what the law now grants him.

chapters.title: Book IV. CHAP. VI. Of the Dictature.
paragraphs: Laws that never bend to circumstances can sometimes do harm and, at a critical moment, ruin the state. The required procedures and formalities take time that events do not always allow. A thousand situations may arise that the legislature never anticipated. It is essential to understand that no law can provide for everything especially when a crisis arrives without warning.
We should not make laws so rigid that they cannot be suspended. Even Sparta sometimes let its laws lie dormant temporarily.

Nothing but the certainty of greater danger should lead a people to change its government, and the sacred force of law should never be restrained unless public safety is at stake. In an unusual crisis when danger is unmistakable, a particular decision may entrust its management to the people best suited for the task. This commission can be granted in two ways, depending on the kind of danger.

If the situation only requires the government to act more quickly, authority should be given to one or two of its members. This changes the administrative form, not the force of the laws. But if legal procedures would prevent a remedy to the danger, a supreme leader may be appointed to silence the laws and suspend sovereign authority for a time. In that case the people’s general will is clear: their main purpose must be saving the state from destruction. Temporarily suspending legislative authority does not abolish it. The magistrate who silences it cannot make it speak; he can override it but cannot represent it. He may do anything except make laws.

The first method was used by Rome’s Senate when it gave the consuls solemn instructions to protect the commonwealth. The second was used when one consul appointed a dictator, a custom Rome borrowed from Alba within the republic.
The appointment was made secretly at night, as if the Romans were ashamed to put one person so far above the laws.

Early in the republic, the Romans often used a dictatorship because the state was not yet stable enough to support itself through its constitution. The people’s customs also made later precautions unnecessary: nobody feared that the dictator would abuse his authority or try to keep it past the appointed term. In fact, the immense power seemed a burden to those who received it, and they were eager to give it up—as if standing above the law were a difficult and dangerous job by design as a lasting burden.

What people criticized in ancient times was not the danger of abuse but the degradation of this supreme office. When it was used for elections and other formalities, it was rightly feared that people would respect it less in genuine emergencies. They might come to see as merely ceremonial a position created to help with empty rituals This concern was about preserving the office’s public dignity through repeated use.

Near the republic’s end, the Romans were cautious about appointing dictators, after having once used them too freely. Their fear was misplaced. Rome’s weakened capital protected it against magistrates within the city. In some cases a dictator could have defended public liberty without seizing it. Rome’s chains were forged not in the city but in its armies abroad. How little authority the city could wield against outside force was shown by Marius’s weak resistance to Sylla and Pompey’s to Caesar during moments of foreign pressure abroad.

This mistake led to serious errors, such as failing to name a dictator during Catiline’s conspiracy. Since the danger involved only the city or at most a province of Italy, a dictator with the unlimited authority granted by law could easily have broken up the plot. Instead it was suppressed only through a series of fortunate events that no human foresight could have expected. The Senate merely placed all its power in the consuls’ hands. To act effectively, Cicero then had to exceed his authority at a critical moment. Though the public first applauded him in their excitement, he was later rightly called to account for shedding blood in violation of the laws—an accusation nobody could have made against a dictator. The consul’s eloquence carried the day. A Roman who valued his personal glory above his country’s, Cicero thought less about the most lawful and certain way to save the state than about securing all the credit for himself. He was rightly honoured as Rome’s saviour and rightly punished as a breaker of its laws. However glorious his action seemed, he was granted an exception.
He could not know this when he proposed naming a dictator: he dared not nominate himself and could not be sure his colleague would appoint him.

However this important commission is granted, its duration must be brief and must never be extended. When a crisis makes a dictator necessary, the state is either saved or lost quickly. Once the danger has passed, dictatorship becomes useless and tyrannical. Roman dictators served for only six months, and most resigned before the term ended. If their term had been longer, they might have tried to lengthen it again, as the decemvir did when his office lasted a full year. A dictator received only the time needed to complete the task for which he was appointed, leaving no time to devise other schemes for that emergency.

chapters.title: Book IV. CHAP. VII. Of the Censorship.
paragraphs: Laws declare the general will; censorship declares the public judgment. Public opinion is a kind of law that the censor applies to particular cases, following the prince’s example The censor gives official form to judgments held by the public.
The censorial court does not decide what the people should think; it merely states what they already think. Whenever it departs from public opinion, its decisions are empty and ineffective.

It is useless to classify a people’s customs by the things they esteem, since all such judgments come from the same source and are necessarily entangled. Everywhere, people’s opinions, not nature, determine which pleasures they choose. Correct their prejudices and opinions, and their habits will correct themselves. We always admire what is beautiful, or what seems beautiful, but our judgment may be mistaken; that is what must be regulated. Whoever judges people’s customs claims to judge honour, and whoever judges honour makes that decision based on opinion.

People’s opinions depend on their constitution. Laws may not control customs directly, but the legislature gives rise to them. When legislative authority grows weak, customs decay; censors then cannot accomplish what the laws themselves failed to do over time.

The office of censor may therefore preserve customs, but it can never restore them once lost. Censors must be established while the laws are strong. Once that strength has gone, the work is finished; no legal measure can have effect when the laws have lost their force.

Censors preserve customs by preventing opinions from becoming corrupt, maintaining what is decent and proper through sound judgments, and sometimes settling opinions when they are uncertain. In France, the practice of bringing seconds to duels had become excessive. A royal decree ended it at once by inserting the words: “As for those who have the cowardice to call themselves seconds.” This judgment anticipated public opinion and worked. The same decrees called it cowardly to fight a duel. That was true, but it contradicted popular opinion, so people laughed at the decision as a public response.

I have said elsewhere that public opinion is subject to no constraint, so it should not appear to be constrained by the court that represents it. We can only admire how skilfully the Romans—and even more effectively the Spartans—used this force, which modern peoples have entirely neglected.
I will only touch here on a point I have discussed at greater length in my letter to Monsieur d’Alembert.

A man of poor character once made an excellent proposal in Sparta’s council. The ephors ignored him and asked a respected, virtuous citizen to present the same proposal. How honouring to the second man and humiliating to the first—without directly praising or blaming either! Some Samians behaved indecently while appearing before the ephors. The next day, a public decree allowed the Samians to become slaves. Would an actual punishment have been harsher than this impunity? Once the Spartans had publicly judged some conduct decent or indecent, all Greece accepted their judgment.

chapters.title: Book IV. CHAP. VIII. Of political Religion.
paragraphs: In the earliest ages, people had no kings but gods and no government except theocratic rule. Their feelings and ideas had to change greatly before they could bring themselves to regard another human being as a master and believe they could live well under that arrangement.

Since each political community placed a deity at its head, each people had its own gods. Two communities that knew little of each other and were usually at odds could not long recognize one master. Nor could two armies facing one another in battle obey the same commander. Polytheism therefore followed naturally from the division of nations, as did the lack of both civic and religious tolerance, which are in fact the same thing, as I will show later.

The Greeks’ claim to find their own gods among those of other nations clearly arose from their ambition to be seen as those peoples’ rightful rulers. Today we regard as a particularly absurd kind of scholarship the attempt to prove that different nations’ gods were the same: that Moloch, Saturn, and Cronos were one deity, or that the Phoenicians’ Baal, the Greeks’ Zeus, and the Latins’ Jupiter were identical. What could imaginary beings with different names possibly have in common in any respect at all!

Why, then, were there no religious wars among the pagans, when each state had its own god and worship? Precisely because religion belonged to the state’s laws and government: people made no distinction between obeying their gods and obeying their laws. Their wars were at once political and religious, and each nation’s gods had authority only within its own borders. One people’s god had no rule over another people, and the pagan gods were not jealous of one another’s rights; they shared humanity’s worship peacefully. Moses himself sometimes speaks this way of Israel’s god. The Hebrews did despise the gods of the Canaanites, a people condemned to destruction whose land was given to them as an inheritance. But they speak more respectfully of neighbouring peoples’ deities, whom they were forbidden to attack. “Will you not possess,” Jephthah asks Sihon, king of the Ammonites, “what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? So we shall possess whatever the Lord our God drives out before us.” I think this passage recognizes that Chemosh and Israel’s god had similar claims.

When the Jews later came under the kings of Babylon and then Syria and refused to recognize any god but their own, their conquerors viewed this refusal as rebellion. It brought on the persecutions described in their history, with no known parallel before Christianity arose under foreign rulers.
The Phocian conflict called the Sacred War was not, strictly speaking, a religious war. It aimed to punish sacrilege, not to conquer unbelievers.

Because every people’s religion was bound exclusively to its state’s laws, the only way to convert a nation was to conquer it. Warriors were the only missionaries, and the conquered had to adopt the victor’s religion as a law. They had to be defeated before anyone asked them to change their faith. People did not fight for their gods; their gods, like Homer’s, fought on people’s behalf. Each people asked its own deity for victory and thanked it by building more altars. Before laying siege to a fortress, the Romans called on its gods to abandon it. When they left Tarentum’s people with their angry deities, they plainly regarded those gods as conquered and owing homage to Rome’s. They allowed the defeated to keep their religion as they sometimes let them keep their laws; often the only tribute they demanded was a wreath for Jupiter Capitolinus.

As Rome spread its empire, it spread its religion too, sometimes even adopting the defeated people’s gods. The peoples of this immense empire came to possess a multitude of gods and faiths, and because their pagan beliefs did not differ fundamentally, paganism gradually became one religion throughout the world.

Things stood this way when Jesus came to establish a spiritual kingdom on earth. By separating religious from political rule, this idea necessarily created the internal divisions that have continued to trouble Christianity. The pagans had never imagined a kingdom in another world. They viewed Christians as rebels who, under a false show of humility, were merely waiting for the right moment to become independent and skilfully seize the authority they pretended to respect while weak and new. This was surely why Christians were persecuted.

In time what the pagans feared actually happened. Everything changed: as their numbers grew, the meek Christians changed their tone, and their invisible kingdom in another world became, under a visible ruler, the most despotic and tyrannical kingdom in this one.

Every country also had civil rulers and laws. These two powers therefore struggled constantly over jurisdiction, making a sound system of domestic government almost impossible in Christian states. We can never settle whether prince or priest is the one we must obey in practice.

Some peoples, in Europe and nearby, have tried to preserve or restore the old arrangement, without success: Christianity’s influence has prevailed everywhere. Religious worship has remained, or again become, independent of the sovereign and no longer necessarily connected to the political body. Muhammad had sound and coherent plans for government. While his system operated under the caliphs and their successors, it remained consistent and, in this respect, good. But as the Arabs became wealthy, learned, refined, idle, and cowardly, they were conquered by barbarians. Then the division between religious and political power returned. It is less obvious among Muslims than among Christians, but can still be seen, especially in Ali’s sect. In some states, such as Persia, this division is always clear.

The kings of England, like the tsars of Russia, stand at the head of their churches. By this title, however, they are more ministers than masters of religion: they cannot change it, only maintain its existing form. Wherever clergy form a collective body, they become both masters and lawmakers in their own cause. England and Russia therefore have two sovereigns, as do other states under their current kings.

It is not so much the clergy’s formal meetings, such as those held in France, that unite them as one body as the communion shared among their churches. Communion and excommunication form the clergy’s social compact, through which they always maintain power over kings and people. Priests in communion with one another are fellow citizens, even when they live at opposite ends of the world. This is a masterly political invention. Pagan priests had nothing like it and never formed a clerical body.

Among Christian writers, only Mr. Hobbes recognized both the problem and its remedy, and dared to recommend joining these two heads of the eagle again, restoring the political unity without which no state or government can be well formed. But he should have understood that Christianity’s prevailing spirit was incompatible with his plan and that the Church’s interests would always outweigh the state’s. His book was hated less for what was false and offensive than for what was just and true here.

Grotius’s letter to his brother dated 11 April 1643 shows what that great jurist praised and criticized in *De Cive*. Grotius was forgiving and seems willing to overlook the book’s faults because of its merits; the rest of the world was less generous in both the text and its argument.

I think a proper display of historical evidence from this perspective could easily refute both Bayle and Warburton. Bayle claims that no religion can help a political body; Warburton claims that Christianity is its best and firmest support. Against the first, we could show that every state was founded on religion. Against the second, we could show that Christianity’s teachings ultimately weaken the state more than they strengthen it through historical cases and could be weighed fairly.
To make my point fully clear, I need only give greater precision to the vague ideas people generally have about political religion.

Religion as it relates to society, whether generally or in a particular community, falls into two kinds: the religion of the individual and the religion of the citizen. The first has no temples, altars, or rituals. It is purely an inward worship of the supreme being and the practice of eternal moral duties: the pure, simple religion of the Gospel, genuine theism, which we may call natural divine law. The second belongs to one country alone, whose gods and protecting saints are unique to it. It consists of doctrines, rites, and outward forms of worship required by that country’s laws. Everyone from another country is considered an unbeliever, foreigner, and barbarian. This religion extends human duties and rights no farther than its own altars. Such were all the religions of the earliest ages; we may call them civil or positive divine law.

There is a third, even stranger kind of religion. It divides society between two legislatures, two leaders, and two parties, giving people duties that conflict and preventing them from being at once worshippers and citizens. Such are the religions of the Lamas, the Japanese, and Roman Catholics. It could be called the religion of priests; it imposes a mixed, antisocial set of duties for which we have no name.

Considered politically, all three kinds of religion have flaws. The third is so plainly defective that there is no need to discuss its faults at length. Anything that breaks the social bond is worthless; any institution that turns people against themselves serves no purpose here.

The second kind deserves some praise because it joins worship of the gods with respect for the laws. By making the country itself an object of devotion, it teaches citizens that serving the state means serving its protecting deity. This is a form of theocracy in which the prince alone should be pontiff and magistrates alone should be priests. To die for one’s country in such a state is martyrdom; breaking the laws is impiety; and condemning a criminal to public shame means delivering him to divine anger.

Yet this religion is blameworthy because it rests on falsehood and deceit, misleads people, and makes them gullible and superstitious. It replaces true worship with empty ceremonies. It is also exclusive and tyrannical, making people violent and persecuting, so that a nation may breathe only murder and massacre while believing it performs a holy act by killing those who worship differently. Such a people is naturally at war with every other nation, to its own great peril It treats differences of worship as threats to public order It treats differences of worship as threats to public order.

The only kind left is Christianity’s rational, humane religion—not as people practise it today, but as it appears in the Gospel, which is quite different. According to this holy, elevated, true faith, all people are children of one God and recognize one another as siblings. The society that binds them lasts until death.

But because this religion has no particular tie to the political body, it leaves the laws with no more strength than they had before, adding nothing to them. It therefore does nothing to strengthen the bonds of a particular society. Christianity does not attach citizens’ hearts to the state; it turns them away from it and from worldly affairs generally. Nothing could be more contrary to the spirit of society.

People say that a nation of true Christians would be the most perfect society imaginable. There is one serious objection: a society of true Christians would not be a society of human beings. I will go further: despite its perfection, such a society would be neither strongest nor most durable. Because it would be perfect, it would lack the strongest bonds of connection, and that very lack would destroy it.

Individuals might do their duty; the people might obey the laws; their leaders might be fair, their magistrates honest, and their soldiers unafraid of death. Vanity and luxury might be absent. Everything would seem to go well. But let us consider further.

Christianity is a spiritual faith concerned only with heaven; a Christian’s inheritance is not in this world. He does his duty, certainly, but he is deeply indifferent to whether his efforts succeed or fail. If he has nothing to blame himself for, it matters little to him whether things go well or badly here below. If the state prospers, he can hardly rejoice in its happiness for fear of becoming proud of his country’s glory. If it declines, he blesses God for bringing his people low.

Social peace and harmony also require that every citizen, without exception, be an equally good Christian. If even one is ambitious or hypocritical, if there is a Catiline or Cromwell among them, he will surely prey easily on his pious fellow citizens. Christian charity makes it hard to think ill of one’s neighbour. The moment someone discovers how to deceive the majority and receives some public authority, he becomes a dignitary. Christians must not speak badly of those in office; respected in this way, he gains power. Christians must obey higher authorities. If someone entrusted with power abuses it, he becomes the rod God uses to punish his children.

Even if their consciences allowed Christians to expel a usurper, that would break the public peace and lead to violence and bloodshed—hardly consistent with true Christian meekness. And in this valley of misery, does it matter to them whether they are free or enslaved? Their true concern is saving their souls and gaining happiness in another world; to achieve that, they are taught to accept their condition here.

Suppose such a state is forced into war with a neighbouring power. Its citizens might march into battle without trying to flee and perform their duty on the field, but they would have no eagerness to win; they have been taught that dying is better than conquering. What difference does victory or defeat make to them? Think what advantages an aggressive, enthusiastic enemy could seize from their stoicism! Put them against a brave, generous people filled with love of glory and country—say, a truly Christian republic against Sparta or Rome. The Christians would be beaten, routed, and cut down before they knew what was happening; their only protection would be their enemy’s contempt for them. Fabius’s soldiers swore a fine oath: they did not promise to die or to win, but swore they would return victorious, and they kept their promise. Christian troops could not swear this; they would fear putting the Lord their God to the test.

But I have made a mistake by speaking of a Christian republic: one of these terms necessarily excludes the other. Christianity teaches submission and dependence. Its spirit is too favourable to tyrants for them not to take advantage of it. True Christians are made for slavery, they know it, and they never concern themselves with conspiracies or revolts; this passing life means too little to them.

Will someone say that Christians make excellent soldiers? I deny it. Show me your Christian troops. I know of no truly Christian soldiers. Do you name the Crusaders? Whatever their courage, they were far from being Christian citizens. They were the priest’s soldiers, citizens of the Church, fighting for a spiritual homeland that the Church had somehow turned into a worldly one. This was a return to paganism. Since the Gospel founded no national religion, true Christians could never wage a holy war to the faith Their claimed spiritual purpose also serves as political rule.

Christian soldiers under pagan emperors were brave, as every Christian writer assures us—and I believe them. Their courage came from honour or rivalry stirred by the pagan troops. When the emperors became Christian, that rivalry vanished. Once the cross had driven out the eagle, Roman courage disappeared in the empire.

Setting political questions aside, let us return to the question of right and establish the proper principles for this important matter. The social compact gives the sovereign authority only as far as public benefit requires. A subject is therefore not answerable to the sovereign for beliefs that have nothing to do with the community. It matters greatly to the state that each citizen hold a religion that inspires respect for duty. But that religion’s beliefs concern the community only insofar as they affect morals and the obligations people owe their fellow citizens. Beyond that, each person may profess whatever beliefs he wishes, and the sovereign has no right to interfere. It has no authority over the next world; it does not matter to the sovereign what happens to citizens after death, provided they fulfil their duties in this life.

The Marquis d’A. says that in a republic everyone is perfectly free because nobody may harm another. This is the firm boundary of republican liberty, and it could not be stated more exactly. I cannot resist quoting this unpublished manuscript from time to time to honour a respected and distinguished person who preserved his integrity as a citizen while serving in government and adopted the most honest, beneficial policies for his country.

There is therefore a purely civic profession of faith, whose principles the sovereign may establish—not as religious beliefs but as sentiments required by society, without which a person cannot be a good citizen or faithful subject. The sovereign may justly expel someone who refuses these sentiments, but not for impiety: he is unsociable, unable to sincerely value justice or sacrifice his life when duty requires. If someone publicly professes these sentiments and then behaves as though he rejects them, he may justly be put to death for the greatest of crimes: denying what he holds in his heart before the laws in all cases.

When Caesar argued for Catiline, he tried to establish that the soul is mortal. Cato and Cicero did not answer with a philosophical debate. They showed instead that Caesar spoke like a bad citizen and advanced a doctrine dangerous to the state. That was the only matter before Rome’s Senate; theology was not in question in the Senate itself.

The principles of civic religion should be few and simple, stated precisely, with no explanations or commentary. Its positive beliefs should be: that a powerful, intelligent, benevolent, all-knowing, provident deity exists; that there is an afterlife; that the virtuous are rewarded and the wicked punished; and that the social compact and laws are sacred. For a negative belief, I would include only one: persecution is forbidden.

In my view, those who distinguish civil tolerance from religious tolerance are mistaken. We cannot live in sincere peace with people we firmly believe are condemned. To love them would seem to mean hating God for punishing them, so we must either persecute or convert them. Wherever religious persecution exists, it inevitably affects civil government. The sovereign then ceases to be sovereign even in worldly matters: priests become the real masters and kings merely their agents in any way.

Modern governments cannot maintain one exclusive national religion. They must therefore tolerate every religion that is itself tolerant of others, provided its beliefs do not conflict with the duties of a good citizen. Anyone who dares to say, “There is no salvation outside our church,” should be expelled from the state, unless the state itself is religious and its prince a pontiff. This doctrine is useful only under theocracy; everywhere else it is destructive. The reason Henry IV is said to have given for converting to Roman Catholicism should have made an honest person reject that faith—and especially a prince capable of thinking clearly.

chapters.title: Book IV. CHAP. IX. The Conclusion.
paragraphs: Having laid out the true principles of political law and tried to set the state on a proper foundation, I must now show how external relations sustain it.

This would include the law of nations and commerce, rules of war and conquest, alliances, negotiations, treaties, and related matters. But these open a new field too broad for so brief a view as mine; I must stay with subjects nearer at hand and better suited to my limited abilities.
